title: The Energy Problem

beats.narrativeText: Lights flicker and systems keep cutting out — the outpost's power shortages haven't gone away, and it's finally time to solve them properly.
The tempting solution — turn everything back on at once — isn't actually an option. There isn't enough power for that, and the station has no way to safely absorb the mistake.
The learner analyses how electricity is distributed through the station and what each system genuinely requires to run.
Working through a series of circuit challenges, the learner starts to see how the station's power network actually connects, system to system.
The learner must decide which systems matter most and weigh that against exactly how much energy is actually available — not everything can come back on at once.
Piece by piece, the learner works out a sequence that can safely bring power back — not the fastest possible order, but the one that won't cause another failure.
The learner records their reasoning for why each system was prioritised in that order — the sequence only means something if it can be explained.

Major systems return online, one by one. But the evidence doesn't just show a station running out of power — it shows one that was deliberately conserving it, on purpose, for a reason still unexplained.

activities.title: Analyse Energy Requirements
activities.storyContext: Every system at Outpost Echo draws a different amount of power — the first step is knowing exactly how much each one actually needs.
activities.instructions: Work out how much energy each station system requires to operate, one system at a time.
activities.output: A list of energy requirements for each system.

activities.title: Solve Circuit Challenges
activities.storyContext: The station's power network connects every system together — restore one link carelessly, and you risk the ones depending on it too.
activities.instructions: Solve a series of circuit challenges to work out exactly how the power network is connected, system by system.
activities.output: Solved circuit challenges showing the power network layout.

activities.title: Prioritise Essential Systems
activities.storyContext: Turning everything on isn't an option — the learner has to decide what actually matters most with the energy that's genuinely available.
activities.instructions: Decide which systems should be restored first, given the limited energy available, and be ready to defend the order you choose.
activities.output: A prioritised list of systems to restore.

activities.title: Record Reasoning
activities.storyContext: A good plan can always be explained — if the reasoning only lives in your head, it isn't really finished yet.
activities.instructions: Write down the reasoning behind your restoration sequence, system by system, not just the final order.
activities.output: A written explanation of the restoration sequence.

activities.title: Design an Emergency Power Plan
activities.storyContext: A good Explorer plans ahead for the next emergency, not just the current one.
activities.instructions: Design an emergency power plan for the station in case of a future shortage.

activities.title: Electricity in Extreme Environments
activities.storyContext: Outpost Echo isn't the only remote station that has to solve power problems.
activities.instructions: Find out how remote research stations generate electricity in extreme environments.
activities.output: None required — this is an open investigation.

prompts: How did you decide which systems to restore first, and what would have gone wrong if you'd chosen a different order?

discussionPoints: Why is it important to prioritise which systems to restore first?
What would happen if every system was restored at once?
parentGuide.assessment: Look for a restoration sequence that is justified by reasoning about priorities, not a random order.

completionCriteria: Energy requirements analysed, circuit challenges solved, and essential systems prioritised with recorded reasoning.
